analysis.headline: Passed the House 357-70 on Jan 31, 2024, but a Senate procedural vote on Aug 1, 2024 failed 48-44 — short of the 60 needed to begin debate — and the Senate never took up the bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a bipartisan tax package. It would have increased the refundable child tax credit to $1,800 per child (2023), $1,900 (2024), and $2,000 (2025) and counted it per child instead of per family, so larger low-income families would get more. It also let families whose income dropped use their prior year's earnings for the child tax credit and Earned Income Tax Credit, made compensation payments to East Palestine, Ohio train derailment victims and certain wildfire victims tax-free, expanded the low-income housing tax credit, and restored business tax breaks like immediate deducting of research costs and 100% bonus depreciation through 2025-2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with children (a larger, per-child refundable credit and a rule letting families with a bad year use the prior year's income); victims of the East Palestine, Ohio derailment and of federally declared wildfires, whose compensation payments would not be taxed; residents of areas needing affordable housing (a 12.5% bigger low-income housing tax credit and easier bond financing); small businesses and contractors (a higher $1,000 1099 reporting threshold, restored research-expensing, extended bonus depreciation, and higher equipment-expensing limits); and U.S. companies and workers dealing with Taiwan through reduced double taxation. [S3][S5]

how_it_helps.text: The maximum refundable child tax credit rises to $1,800 in 2023, $1,900 in 2024, and $2,000 in 2025, and the refundable amount is multiplied by the number of qualifying children, so a family with two or three children gets a proportionally larger credit instead of the credit phasing in at the same pace as a one-child family.

Families whose earned income falls in 2024 or 2025 could elect to use the prior year's earned income when calculating the child tax credit and earned income tax credit, cushioning a job loss or cut in hours.
People who already filed their 2023 returns before the change would have the IRS recalculate the credit and refund the difference as quickly as possible.

Compensation for losses from federally declared wildfires (payments received 2020-2025) and from the February 3, 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment — including from Norfolk Southern, its insurers, and government agencies — would be excluded from taxable income.

The low-income housing tax credit ceiling increases by 12.5% for 2023-2025 and the bond-financing threshold drops to 30% for projects financed before 2026, making more affordable-housing projects financially viable.

Businesses could again immediately deduct domestic research costs incurred through 2025 instead of spreading them over five years, 100% bonus depreciation is extended through 2026, and equipment-expensing limits rise from $1 million to $1.29 million — relief aimed at companies investing in growth, including small firms.
The 1099 reporting threshold for payments to independent contractors rises from $600 to $1,000 (with inflation adjustments), reducing paperwork for small businesses and freelancers.

analysis.who_pays: The clearest concentrated cost falls on promoters of COVID-era employee retention credit claims: the bill sets a January 31, 2024 deadline for claiming the credit and imposes new penalties on promoters — up to the greater of $200,000 ($10,000 for individuals) or 75% of the promoter's gross income from the advice, plus $1,000 per due-diligence failure. [S5] Beyond that, the main cost is diffuse rather than concentrated: the Treasury collects less (higher child tax credits, extended business deductions, reduced withholding on Taiwan residents), with the ERTC deadline and penalties as partial offsets. No major industry bears a visible cost in the bill text, which is consistent with the wide, mostly bipartisan House support. [S3][S5][S8]

drawbacks.text: The family, disaster, and housing provisions are all temporary — the child tax credit increases and housing credit expansion run only through 2025, and the business provisions through 2025-2026 — so the benefits would lapse unless Congress acted again.

Three of the bill's six titles are business tax cuts (research expensing, bonus depreciation, equipment expensing, Taiwan double-tax relief), so a substantial share of the cost goes to tax reductions for companies rather than directly to households.

The anti-fraud title has real teeth aimed at a specific group: claims for COVID-era employee retention credits are cut off after January 31, 2024, and promoters face penalties of up to $200,000 or 75% of their gross income — a cost borne by that industry and by taxpayers who missed the deadline.

The bill was not uncontroversial even in the House: 70 members voted against final passage, including 47 Republicans, and in the Senate 41 of the 44 votes against starting debate were Republicans, showing substantial minority-party opposition despite the bipartisan negotiation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary families this was a genuinely helpful but modest and temporary package: a bigger refundable child credit for low-income working parents, tax-free disaster compensation, and more affordable-housing capacity, alongside larger and costlier business tax cuts. The design is conventional rather than transformative — everything sunsets within a few years, and the business titles take up half the bill. Its fatal weakness was not its content but its path: after passing the House 357-70, it died on a Senate procedural vote, so none of these benefits were delivered.

outcome.mechanism: A Senate procedural vote (cloture on the motion to proceed) failed 48-44 on August 1, 2024 — 12 votes short of the 60 needed — so the Senate never debated the bill, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 17, 2024 by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO), chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, and referred to Ways and Means.
The Ways and Means Committee marked it up on January 19 and reported it amended by a vote of 40-3; the Rules Committee was discharged on January 23 and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar.

On January 31, 2024 the House passed it 357-70 under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — 188 Democrats and 169 Republicans in favor, 23 Democrats and 47 Republicans against.

The Senate received the bill February 1, 2024, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 349) on March 21 — it was never referred to a Senate committee.
On July 29, 2024, Majority Leader Chuck Schumer made a motion to proceed to the bill and filed a cloture motion — the first step toward getting Senate floor time.

On August 1, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 48-44: 43 Democrats and 2 independents voted yes, but only 3 Republicans did, with 41 Republicans voting no. Failing this vote meant the Senate could not begin debating the bill.
Schumer made a motion to reconsider the failed vote, but no further Senate action followed, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill never receiving a Senate vote.

key_actors.name: Jason Smith
key_actors.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee; bill sponsor
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through committee markup (reported 40-3 in two days), and managed House floor passage under suspension of the rules, 357-70.

key_actors.name: Chuck Schumer
key_actors.what_they_did: Made the motion to proceed to the bill and filed the cloture motion in July 2024, then moved to reconsider after the cloture vote failed; the Senate never reached the bill again.

key_actors.name: Senate Republicans
key_actors.what_they_did: Supplied 41 of the 44 votes against cloture on the motion to proceed on August 1, 2024, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate.

key_actors.name: House Ways and Means Committee
key_actors.what_they_did: Held markup on January 19, 2024, and reported the amended bill 40-3, clearing the way for floor action within two weeks of introduction.
